issues.explanation: 'Avoid Exercise' is not clinically coherent with the rest of the profile. The threat items center on hypervigilance about nighttime intrusion and safety checking in the home, while the memory and appraisal items focus on intrusive assault memories, danger, and physical vulnerability. Exercise avoidance addresses a different symptom domain and lacks plausible linkage to the selected threat, memory, or appraisal content. In contrast, magical thinking and mirror checking fit better with maladaptive attempts to manage threat and distress.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Physical Vulnerability: My body has been permanently damaged by what happened
issues.explanation: These two selected items are difficult to reconcile within the same profile. A strong appraisal of permanent bodily damage implies acknowledgment of serious ongoing physical consequences, whereas telling oneself the event did not really happen or was not that bad reflects minimization/denial of the trauma's reality or impact. While some ambivalence can occur clinically, this pair pulls in opposing directions strongly enough to question internal coherence in this profile.

vignette:
Grace is a 78-year-old widow, a potter who has spent most of her life shaping clay in the small studio attached to her home. Eighteen months ago, that home became the site of an assault. A man broke in through the back door just after dusk, while she was kneading a batch of terracotta. He grabbed her from behind, threw her to the floor, and pressed a knife against her throat before fleeing with her purse. She remembers the gritty feel of the concrete floor against her cheek, the smell of his sweat, the weight of his knee on her spine. She managed to call 911, but in the months since, the world has rearranged itself around that moment.

The memory forces its way into her mind without warning—a flash of the knife blade, the sound of his breathing, the crushing pressure on her back. When it comes, she feels as though she is right back on that studio floor, her heart slamming, her body rigid. These images are mostly pictures, vivid and wordless, and they arrive whether she is at her wheel or lying in bed. She has tried to push them away, convinced that if she lets herself think about the assault she will be overwhelmed, that she cannot handle what she might feel. But that conviction—that she was too fragile to bear it—was itself what summoned the memory most sharply: the knife blade, the weight on her back, as if her mind were proving her right by showing her exactly what she could not face. So she suppresses the thoughts, but they break through anyway, and each intrusion deepens her belief that the world is fundamentally dangerous and that her own body has turned against her—it keeps reacting as if the danger is still present, even when she knows she is safe.

That belief—that the world is dangerous—has come to organize her days. She now checks the locks on every door and window three or four times before she can sit down to dinner, and again before bed. She has taken to checking mirrors in every room, scanning the reflection for someone who might be behind her. The checking feels momentarily necessary, but it also reinforces her sense of threat: if she needs to check, the danger must be real. She listens constantly for sounds that might mean someone is entering her home—a creak, a footstep, the click of a latch—and she wakes during the night to check again, unable to relax even when she knows the doors are bolted. That nocturnal vigilance, the listening and the waking, drives her to perform another round of lock checks, which only confirms that she was right to be watchful.

Her pottery studio has become a place of dread. She used to find solace in the rhythm of the wheel, but now the concrete floor, the dim light, the back door that leads to the alley—all of it pulls her back into the memory. She has reduced her hours, stopped taking custom orders, and avoids working after four in the afternoon. When she does force herself to throw a pot, an intrusive image of the attacker’s hand on her shoulder will surface, and she will have to stop, wiping clay from her shaking fingers. That reliving experience, in turn, strengthens her fearful appraisal: if even her own studio is unsafe, then the world is indeed dangerous, and her body is not to be trusted. She has come to see her own physiological reactions—the racing heart, the trembling—as evidence that she is still in peril, which makes her monitor her surroundings even more closely.

The cycle has tightened over the months. Her checking and her thought suppression were meant to give her control, but they have only made her more convinced that she cannot cope, that the memory is too powerful to face. She now avoids mirrors because the movement in the reflection startles her; she avoids nightfall because the shadows trigger her listening; she avoids thinking about the assault, yet the visual memories intrude with increasing frequency, each one confirming that her efforts are failing. The consequence has been a shrinking life. Her daughter has noticed she no longer answers the phone after dark, that her kiln sits cold for weeks. Grace knows something is wrong, but what finally brought her to seek help was a morning last week when she found herself checking the front door lock seventeen times before she could leave for a doctor’s appointment. She is afraid that if she does not get a handle on this, she will lose the last thing that still matters—her ability to work the clay that has anchored her for sixty years. She hopes, quietly, that talking about the memory might somehow loosen its grip, even as she fears that doing so will shatter her.

violations.explanation: The vignette does not convey that negative appraisals lead to memory intrusions; instead, memory intrusions are shown to trigger or strengthen negative appraisals.

vignette_attempts.feedback:
REQUIRED EDGES MISSING:
- Negative Appraisals → Memory: The vignette does not convey that negative appraisals lead to memory intrusions; instead, memory intrusions are shown to trigger or strengthen negative appraisals.
  e.g. "The belief that she was permanently changed kept bringing her back to the moment it had happened, as if she needed to locate exactly where she had been lost."
  e.g. "Telling herself that she should have seen it coming made the memory more vivid and easier to find — it sat there waiting, proof of her failure."
  e.g. "The conviction that she was weak fed directly into the flashback, colouring it, making it worse: she wasn't just there again, she was there again and helpless."
